The second: He made its learning easy for all people.

As for ﴿He created man﴾ (55:3), there are two opinions:

The first: it refers to Adam. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: He intended all people, even though it is in the singular form. This is the view of most scholars.

The second: good and evil. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: speech and utterance. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: writing, which is reported from the early authorities.

The fifth: guidance. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

An eighth view belongs to some of the people of khawatir (inspirational thinkers): He created man ignorant of it, then taught him the way to it.

The first: it means by calculation. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-husban is a verbal noun of hisab (calculation), and it has been said that it is its plural.

The second: the meaning of al-husban is that these are their terms; when the term ends, the Resurrection comes. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: time is measured by them, for the day is distinguished by the sun and the night by the moon. (p-424) Were either of them to persist, so that time became all night or all day, the measure of time would not be known. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: its meaning is that they run by a decree.

The first: it is the prostration of their shadows. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: it is what is in them of craftsmanship and power that necessitates prostration and submission. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿And He set up the balance﴾ (55:7). Concerning this there are three sayings:

The first: it is the balance with a tongue (pointer), so that people may be fair with one another in rights. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: the balance is the judge.

The third: this was said by Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi: it is justice. From this is the saying of Hassan:

"Yathrib knows that we are in it,
when the matter is confused, its balance."

The first: it is justice, and its transgression is injustice. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it is the balance of weighable things, and its transgression is short-weighing. This was said by Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: "O company of mawali (non-Arab clients), you have been entrusted with two matters by which people before you were destroyed: the measure and the balance."

﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾ (55:9), that is, do not diminish it by short-weighing. It has been said: it is the measure. So injustice, if it is taken to mean justice, and distortion, if it is taken to mean judgment.

﴿And the earth He laid out for the creatures﴾ (55:10), that is, He spread it out and made it level for the creatures (al-anam), so that they may settle upon it and derive sustenance from it.

Concerning al-anam there are three sayings:

The first: they are the people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. There is in this the saying of one of the poets about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

"Blessed of face, through whom rain is sought,
there is none among al-anam equal to him or of his rank."

The second: al-anam are humans and jinn. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: al-anam are all creation of every living being. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. It is so called because it sleeps. The poet said:

"May God bestow favour upon Abu al-Walid and his kin,
the Lord of al-anam, and grant him peace."

The first: "palms with sheaths" are the palm trees, and their sheaths are the fibre at their necks. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it is the trunk of the palm tree, which is enclosed (tukammam) in it as a spathe. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And a remnant, upon which I ate
plants in hard-ground clumps."

The third: it is the enclosed spathe, which is the covering of the fruit. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

(p-426) The fourth: the meaning of "possessors of sheaths" is possessors of excess over everything. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is the crop when it has yellowed and dried.

when the veiled women come out of their curtains?"

when the veiled women come out of their curtains?"

The second: the balance is the judge.

The third: this was said by Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi: it is justice. From this is the saying of Hassan:

"Yathrib knows that we are in it,
when the matter is confused, its balance."

"And a remnant, upon which I ate

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 55, verses 14–25:**

First: it is clay mixed with sand. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is moist clay which, when you squeeze it in your hand, lets water come out between your fingers. This is transmitted from ʿIkrimah.

Third: it is dry clay that makes a ringing sound (ṣalṣalah). This was said by Qatadah.

Fourth: it is hollow clay which, when struck with something, rings out and produces a sound.

Fifth: it is foul-smelling clay. This was said by al-Dahhak, and it is derived from the expression "ṣalla al-laḥm" (the meat rotted) when it became putrid.

The one created from ṣalṣāl like pottery (fakhkhār) is Adam, peace be upon him.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: God created Adam from dust, from clay (ṭīn lāzib, sticky clay). He left him in that state for forty years. Then He made him ring like pottery for forty years. Then He shaped him and left him as a body without a soul for forty years. That makes one hundred and twenty years. Throughout all of this the angels were saying: "Glory be to the One who created you, for a great purpose He created you."

﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions:

First: it is the blaze (lahab) of fire. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is a mixture (khalaṭ) of fire. This was said by Abu ʿUbaydah.

Third: it is the green, yellow and red (lahab) flame that rises above fire when it is kindled, lying between the fire and the smoke. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: it is the unrestrained fire that is not held back. This was said by al-Mubarrad.

Fifth: it is the fire that is agitated, moving back and forth, and it was called "mārij" because of its agitation and the speed of its movement.

Regarding the jinn who was created from a smokeless flame of fire, there are two opinions: (p-429) First: he is the father of the jinn. This was said by Abu Farwah Yaʿqub, from Mujahid. Second: he is Iblis, and this is a transmitted (maʾthūr) opinion.

Regarding the fire from which he was created, there are three opinions:

First: it is from the fire visible among creation. This is the view of the majority.

Second: it is fire that exists between the mountains below the sky, like a thin veil. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Third: it is fire below the veil, from which these thunderbolts come, and from which you see the creation of the sky. This was said by al-Farra'.

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: the two easts are the sunrise of the sun in winter and in summer, and the two wests are the sunset of the sun in winter and in summer. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the two easts are the rising of the sun and of the moon, and the two wests are their setting.

Third: the two easts are dawn and the sun, and the two wests are the sun and the twilight (ghasaq).

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah went beyond these with a fourth opinion: the two easts are the rising of the heart and of the tongue, and the two wests are the setting of the heart and of the tongue.

﴿He released the two seas, meeting side by side﴾. As for the two seas, there are five views concerning them:

First: it is the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the sea of Persia and the sea of Rome. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Third: it is the salty sea and the sweet rivers. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

(p-430) Fourth: it is the sea of the east and the sea of the west, whose two extremities meet.

Fifth: it is the sea of pearls and the sea of coral.

As for ﴿He released (maraja) the two seas﴾, there are three opinions:

First: it means separating the two seas. This was said by Ibn Sakhr.

Second: it means letting the two seas flow. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: it means making the two seas level. This was said by Mujahid.

The root of "maraj" is leaving something loose, as an animal roams freely in pasture (al-marj).

﴿Between them is a barrier they do not transgress﴾. Regarding the barrier that is between them, there are four opinions:

First: it is a partition. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is the breadth of the earth. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: it is what lies between the sky and the earth. This was said by ʿAtiyyah and al-Dahhak.

Fourth: it is the island we are on, which is the Arabian Peninsula. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Regarding His words ﴿they do not transgress﴾ there are three opinions:

First: they do not mix; the sweet water does not flow over the salty, nor the salty over the sweet. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: neither of them transgresses against the other to overpower it. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

Third: they do not transgress by meeting. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and the sense of the sentence is: "He released the two seas, meeting side by side, were it not for the barrier between them that prevents them from meeting."

Sahl said: the two seas are the path of good and the path of evil, and the barrier between them is divine success (tawfīq) and protection (ʿiṣmah).

﴿From them emerge pearls and coral﴾. Regarding coral (marjān) there are four opinions:

First: it is the large and great pearls. This was said by ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbas, and from it is the verse of al-Aʿsha:

؎ From every coral in the sea I bring it out, its current and the mud of the shell have protected it.

(p-431) Second: it is the small pearls. This was said by al-Dahhak and Abu Razin.

Third: it is the red beads like rods. This was said by Ibn Masʿud.

Fourth: it is mixed jewels, derived from "maraj al-shay'" when one mixes a thing.

Regarding His words ﴿From them emerge﴾ there are two views:

First: the intended meaning is one of them, even though the speech has linked it to both.

Second: it emerges from both of them according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas that they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth, because when rainwater falls on the shell of the sea it becomes pearls, so it emerges from both.

There is also a third view: the sweet and the salty may meet, so the sweet acts like the mating partner for the salty, and so it is attributed to both, just as a child is attributed to the male and the female even though the female gives birth to it. Second: they ask Him for the strength to worship. This was said by Ibn ʿAṭāʾ. It was also said that they ask Him for mercy for themselves. This was said by Abu Ṣāliḥ.

Qatadah said: neither the people of the heavens nor the people of the earth can do without Him. Al-Kalbi said: the people of the heavens ask Him specifically for forgiveness for themselves and do not ask Him for provision, while the people of the earth ask Him for both forgiveness and provision.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 55, verses 14–25:**

First: it is clay mixed with sand. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is moist clay which, when you squeeze it in your hand, lets water come out between your fingers. This is transmitted from ʿIkrimah.

Third: it is dry clay that makes a ringing sound (ṣalṣalah). This was said by Qatadah.

Fourth: it is hollow clay which, when struck with something, rings out and produces a sound.

Fifth: it is foul-smelling clay. This was said by al-Dahhak, and it is derived from the expression "ṣalla al-laḥm" (the meat rotted) when it became putrid.

The one created from ṣalṣāl like pottery (fakhkhār) is Adam, peace be upon him.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: God created Adam from dust, from clay (ṭīn lāzib, sticky clay). He left him in that state for forty years. Then He made him ring like pottery for forty years. Then He shaped him and left him as a body without a soul for forty years. That makes one hundred and twenty years. Throughout all of this the angels were saying: "Glory be to the One who created you, for a great purpose He created you."

﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions:

First: it is the blaze (lahab) of fire. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is a mixture (khalaṭ) of fire. This was said by Abu ʿUbaydah.

Third: it is the green, yellow and red (lahab) flame that rises above fire when it is kindled, lying between the fire and the smoke. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: it is the unrestrained fire that is not held back. This was said by al-Mubarrad.

Fifth: it is the fire that is agitated, moving back and forth, and it was called "mārij" because of its agitation and the speed of its movement.

Regarding the jinn who was created from a smokeless flame of fire, there are two opinions: (p-429) First: he is the father of the jinn. This was said by Abu Farwah Yaʿqub, from Mujahid. Second: he is Iblis, and this is a transmitted (maʾthūr) opinion.

Regarding the fire from which he was created, there are three opinions:

First: it is from the fire visible among creation. This is the view of the majority.

Second: it is fire that exists between the mountains below the sky, like a thin veil. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Third: it is fire below the veil, from which these thunderbolts come, and from which you see the creation of the sky. This was said by al-Farra'.

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: the two easts are the sunrise of the sun in winter and in summer, and the two wests are the sunset of the sun in winter and in summer. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the two easts are the rising of the sun and of the moon, and the two wests are their setting.

Third: the two easts are dawn and the sun, and the two wests are the sun and the twilight (ghasaq).

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah went beyond these with a fourth opinion: the two easts are the rising of the heart and of the tongue, and the two wests are the setting of the heart and of the tongue.

﴿He released the two seas, meeting side by side﴾. As for the two seas, there are five views concerning them:

First: it is the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the sea of Persia and the sea of Rome. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Third: it is the salty sea and the sweet rivers. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

(p-430) Fourth: it is the sea of the east and the sea of the west, whose two extremities meet.

Fifth: it is the sea of pearls and the sea of coral.

As for ﴿He released (maraja) the two seas﴾, there are three opinions:

First: it means separating the two seas. This was said by Ibn Sakhr.

Second: it means letting the two seas flow. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: it means making the two seas level. This was said by Mujahid.

The root of "maraj" is leaving something loose, as an animal roams freely in pasture (al-marj).

﴿Between them is a barrier they do not transgress﴾. Regarding the barrier that is between them, there are four opinions:

First: it is a partition. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: it is the breadth of the earth. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: it is what lies between the sky and the earth. This was said by ʿAtiyyah and al-Dahhak.

Fourth: it is the island we are on, which is the Arabian Peninsula. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Regarding His words ﴿they do not transgress﴾ there are three opinions:

First: they do not mix; the sweet water does not flow over the salty, nor the salty over the sweet. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: neither of them transgresses against the other to overpower it. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

Third: they do not transgress by meeting. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and the sense of the sentence is: "He released the two seas, meeting side by side, were it not for the barrier between them that prevents them from meeting."

Sahl said: the two seas are the path of good and the path of evil, and the barrier between them is divine success (tawfīq) and protection (ʿiṣmah).

﴿From them emerge pearls and coral﴾. Regarding coral (marjān) there are four opinions:

First: it is the large and great pearls. This was said by ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbas, and from it is the verse of al-Aʿsha:

؎ From every coral in the sea I bring it out, its current and the mud of the shell have protected it.

(p-431) Second: it is the small pearls. This was said by al-Dahhak and Abu Razin.

Third: it is the red beads like rods. This was said by Ibn Masʿud.

Fourth: it is mixed jewels, derived from "maraj al-shay'" when one mixes a thing.

Regarding His words ﴿From them emerge﴾ there are two views:

First: the intended meaning is one of them, even though the speech has linked it to both.

Second: it emerges from both of them according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas that they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth, because when rainwater falls on the shell of the sea it becomes pearls, so it emerges from both.

There is also a third view: the sweet and the salty may meet, so the sweet acts like the mating partner for the salty, and so it is attributed to both, just as a child is attributed to the male and the female even though the female gives birth to it. For this reason it was said that pearls do not come out except from a place where the sweet and the salty meet.

﴿And His are the ships, elevated upon the sea like landmarks﴾. As for "al-jawārī" (the ships), they are the vessels, singular jāriyah, named so because they run (tajrī) on the water by God's permission. Al-jāriyah is also a young woman, and was named so because the water of youth runs in her.

As for "al-munshaʾāt" (elevated), there are five opinions:

First: they are the created things. This was said by Qatadah, derived from "al-inshāʾ" (bringing into being).

Second: they are the laden ones. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: they are the sent ones. This was mentioned by Ibn Kamil.

Fourth: they are the moving ones. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Fifth: they are those whose sails are raised, and these are the ones that are "munshaʾah"; those whose sails are not raised are not "munshaʾah". This was said by al-Kalbi.

Hamzah recited ﴿al-munshiʾāt﴾ with a kasrah on the shīn, and regarding its meaning in this reading there are two views:

First: "the initiators" (al-bādiʾāt). This was said by Ibn Ishaq and al-Jarud ibn Abi Sabrah.

Second: they greatly increase in their rising (nashʾ) through their running and their course on the sea, like landmarks. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Regarding His words ﴿like landmarks﴾ there are two views: (p-432) First: it means the mountains, which were so called because of their height, like the height of landmarks. This was said by al-Suddi.

Al-Khansa' said:

؎ Indeed Sakhr, the guides take their guidance from him, as if he were a beacon with fire on its top.

Second: the landmarks are the palaces. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 55, verses 26–30:

﴿Every day He is in a matter.﴾ On this there are two opinions:

The first: He intends His matter in the two days of this world and the Hereafter. Ibn Bahr said: The whole of time consists of two days:

One of them is the duration of the days of this world, and the other is the Day of Resurrection. So His matter, glorified is He, in the days of this world is trial and testing through command and prohibition, giving life and causing death, giving and withholding. His matter on the Day of Resurrection is recompense, reckoning, reward, and punishment.

The second opinion: What is meant by this is the report of His matter on every day of the days of this world.

Concerning this matter which He intends in the days of this world, there are two opinions:

The first: Whoever among the prophets is sent in every age with what He has legislated for his community of the laws of religion. In this context the matter is the Shari'ah which each prophet legislated in his time, and "day" is an expression for a period of time.

The second opinion: What Allah brings about in His creation of changing conditions and differing affairs, and "day" is an expression for a time.

Mujahid narrated from Ubayd ibn Umayr, who said: "Every day He is in a matter": He answers the one who calls upon Him, gives to the one who asks, relieves the afflicted, accepts the repentance of one people, and forgives another people.

Suwayd ibn Ghafala said: "Every day He is in a matter": He frees necks (slaves), gives to those who desire, and withholds from those who deserve punishment.

Abu al-Darda' narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾: among His matters is that He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises a people, and lowers others."

The first meaning: "We will surely turn to you," in the manner of a threat.

The second meaning: "We will surely intend your reckoning and your recompense for your deeds." This is a warning, because God, exalted is He, is not occupied by one matter so as to be distracted from another. Jarir said:

"Now that you have turned to Numayr, this is the time when you were a torment to them."

That is, you intended them. *Al-thaqalan* (the two weighty ones, meaning mankind and jinn) are so called because they are a burden (*thiql*) upon the earth.

The first: "If you are able to know what is in the heavens and the earth, then know. You will not know it except with authority." This was said by ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 55, verse 37–45:

﴿And when the sky splits open﴾ meaning, on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And it becomes red like a rose﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: the rose of the garden, which is red. Its colours vary, but the most prevalent of its colours is redness, and it is by it that the proverb of redness is struck. ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās said:

"Had I been a rose, whose colour you would love, you would have loved me, but my Lord has disfigured me with my blackness."

Thus the sky will become red like a rose on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn Baḥr.

The second: that by "rose" he meant the rose-coloured horse (al-faras al-ward), which in spring is yellow and in winter is dusty-coloured. So he likened the sky on the Day of Resurrection, in the variation of its colours, to the rose-coloured horse, because of the variation of its colours. This was said by al-Kalbī and al-Farrāʾ.

Regarding His saying ﴿like red oil⁠﴾ [kālddihān] there are five aspects:

The first: it means pure. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The second: clear. This was said by al-Akhfash.

The third: possessing colours. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The fourth: yellow like the colour of oil. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasānī and Abū al-Jawzāʾ.

The fifth: al-dihān is the red surface of the earth. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. al-Aʿshā said:

"And a swift stallion among the noble mares, as if upon his shoulders was a coating of oil."

The earlier scholars claimed that the original colour of the sky is red, and that because of the many barriers and the great distance it appears in this blue colour. They likened this to the veins of the body, which are red like the redness of blood but appear blue through the intervening covering. If this is correct, then on the Day of Resurrection, because the sky will be near the gazes and the barriers will be lifted, it will appear red, because that is the origin of its colour.

﴿So on that Day, neither humans nor jinn will be asked about their sin﴾. Regarding this there are five sayings:

The first: there was questioning before, then their mouths were sealed and their hands and feet spoke of what they used to do. This was said by Qatādah.

The second: that He will not ask them, "Did you do such and such?" This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

The third: He will not ask the angels about them, because they had already lifted up their deeds in the world. This was said by Mujāhid.

The fourth: that some of them will not ask others about their condition, because each one is occupied with himself. This is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The fifth: that on a day in which some faces turn white and some faces turn black, they are recognised by their colours, so they are not asked about. This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

﴿They will circulate between it and scalding hot water, intensely hot﴾. Qatādah said: they will circulate at one time between the scalding water and at another time between the Blazing Fire (al-Jaḥīm); al-Jaḥīm is the fire, and al-Ḥamīm is the drink.

Regarding His saying ﴿intensely hot⁠﴾ [ānin] there are three aspects:

The first: it is that whose heat and scalding have reached their end. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Suddī, and from it is the saying of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī:

"And she dyes a beard that betrayed and deceived, with something red from the blood of the belly, intensely hot (ānin)."

That is, hot.

The second: that it is the present one. This was said by Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb.

The third: that it is the one whose drinking has reached its time and reached its limit. This was said by Mujāhid.

﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. Concerning "the one who fears the standing of his Lord," there are three opinions:

First: he who fears the standing of his Lord after performing the obligatory duties (al-fara'id, the obligatory acts of worship). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: he who intends to commit a sin, then remembers the standing of his Lord and abandons it. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: that this was revealed specifically concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), when he once mentioned Paradise as it was brought near and the Fire as it was made manifest. This was said by 'Ata' and Ibn Shawdhab.

Al-Dahhak said: Rather, one day he drank milk while he was thirsty, and it pleased him. He asked about it and was informed that it was not lawful (min ghayr hill), so he vomited it up, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was watching him. He (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on you. A verse has been revealed concerning you," and he recited this verse to him.

Concerning "the standing of his Lord," there are two opinions:

One: it is a station before the presentation (al-'ardh) and the reckoning (al-hisab).

Two: it is Allah Most High's standing over the accounting of what he has earned of good and evil.

Concerning these two gardens, there are four aspects:

First: the garden of mankind and the garden of the jinn. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: the Garden of Eden (jannat 'adn) and the Garden of Bliss (jannat al-na'im). This was said by Muqatil.

Third: that they are two gardens among the gardens of Paradise. This was narrated as marfu' (traced back to the Prophet), because a bustan (orchard) is called a jannah (garden).

Fourth: that one of the two gardens is his dwelling, and the other is the dwelling of his wives and his servants, as the leaders of this world do.

It also allows a fifth possibility: that one of the two gardens is his dwelling and the other is his orchard.

It also allows a sixth possibility: that one of the two gardens is the lower part of the palaces and the other is their upper part.

﴿Having branches﴾. Concerning this, there are four interpretations:

First: having various colors. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: having various kinds of fruit. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Third: having shade (atan) and spaciousness (si'ah). This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Fourth: having branches (aghsan). This was said by al-Akhfash and Ibn Bahr.

Al-afnan (branches) is the plural of fanan (a single branch), as the poet said:

What stirred your longing is the cooing of a dove,
calling upon the branches of the boughs, calling doves,
calling upon Abu Farkhayn, who encountered a falcon
with two talons, a hawk (qitam) among the falcons.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 55, verses 54–61:**

﴿Reclining on couches whose linings are of brocade.﴾ On this there are two views.

The first: by *bata'inuha* (بَطائِنَها, "its linings") is meant its outer surfaces (*zawahiruha*). This is the view of Qatada.

The Arabs use *al-batn* (البَطْن, "the belly/inside") to mean *al-zahr* (الظَّهْر, "the back/outside"), so they say *hadha batn al-sama'* (هَذا بَطْنُ السَّماءِ, "this is the underside of the sky") and *zahr al-sama'* (ظَهْرُ السَّماءِ, "the upper side of the sky").

The second: he intended the lining (*al-bitana*, البِطانَةَ) and not the outer surface (*al-zihara*, الظِّهارَةِ). This is because, if the lining is of brocade, and the lining is inferior to the outer surface, this indicates that the outer surface is above brocade. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

Abbas was asked, "What are the outer surfaces?" He said: "He only described to you their linings so that your hearts might be guided to it. As for the outer surfaces, none knows them except Allah."

﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near at hand.﴾ As for *al-jana* (الجَنا), it means the fruit. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"This is my fruit and its best, in it, since every picker brings his hand to his mouth."*

Regarding His saying *dani* (دانٍ, "near at hand"), there are two views:

The first: it is near, not distant to one standing or to one sitting. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: neither distance nor thorns prevent their hands from reaching it. This is the view of Qatada.

﴿In them are those restraining their gaze.﴾ Qatada said: "She restricts her gaze to her husband; she does not direct her look at others, nor does she desire any substitute for them."

﴿Untouched before them by man or jinn.﴾ On this there are three views:

The first: "No one has touched them." Abu 'Amr said: "*al-tamth* (الطَّمْث) is touching, and this applies to everything that is touched."

The second: "No man or jinn has tamed them before them." *Al-tamth* is taming (*al-tadhlil*, التَّذْلِيل). This is the view of al-Mubarrad.

The third: "No man or jinn has deflowered them." It is said that *tamth* (طَمْث) is also used for menstruation. Al-Farazdaq said:

*"They were delivered to me, untouched before me, and they are purer than ostrich eggs."*

The verse is evidence that jinn also have intercourse, as men do.

﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ On this there are four views:

The first: is the reward of obedience anything but reward?

The second: is the reward of good in this world anything but good in the Hereafter? This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The third: is the reward of one who testifies that there is no god but Allah anything but Paradise? This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: is the reward of repentance anything but forgiveness? This is the view of Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq.

A fifth view is possible: is the reward of Allah's goodness to you anything but your obedience to Him?

﴿And besides them are two gardens.﴾ On this there are two interpretations:

First: that is, two gardens nearer than those two.

Second: that is, two gardens inferior to them in description.

On this there are three opinions:

First: the four gardens are for the one who fears the standing before his Lord. Ibn ʿAbbas said: in the first two is palm and trees, and in the latter two are crops, plants and what spreads out.

(p-441) Second: the first two are of gold for those brought near (al-muqarrabun), and the latter two are of silver for the companions of the right hand (ashab al-yamin). This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Third: the first two are for the foremost (al-sabiqun), and the latter two are for the followers. This was said by al-Hasan.

Muqatil said: the first two gardens are the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss, and the latter two are the Garden of Firdaws and the Garden of Refuge. Among the four gardens there are many gardens.

A fourth possibility is that ﴿two gardens besides them﴾ are for his followers, because their rank falls short of his rank: one of them is for the maidens with lovely eyes (al-hur al-ʿin), and the other is for the everlasting youths (al-wildan al-mukhalladun), so that males are distinguished from females by them.

﴿dark green﴾ (mudhammatan). On this there are three opinions:

First: that is, both green. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: both blackish. This was said by Mujahid, derived from al-dahmah, which is blackness; and from it horses of black color are called duhm.

Third: [both green from lushness] (khadhrawan min al-rayy), both luxuriant. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿In them are two springs gushing forth.﴾ On this there are three interpretations:

First: both are full and never cease. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: both are flowing. This was said by al-Farra'.

Third: both are spouting. He mentioned in the first two gardens two springs that flow, and mentioned in the latter two gardens two springs that gush forth; and flowing is more than gushing.

With what are they gushing? On this there are four aspects:

First: with water. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: with musk and ambergris. This was said by Anas.

Third: with goodness and blessing. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Kalbi.

Fourth: with kinds of fruit. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

﴿In them are good things and beautiful ones.﴾ That means the four gardens. Regarding the word khayrat (good things), there are two recitations. One of them is with light pronunciation (takhfif), and regarding its intended meaning there are two opinions: (p-442)

First: goodness and favours that are considered beautiful.

Second: good things of fruits and produce, and beautiful (hisan) in appearances and colours.

The second recitation is with emphasis (tashdid) on the letter, khayyirat, and regarding its intended meaning there are two opinions:

First: chosen ones (mukhtarat).

Second: possessors of goodness (dhawat al-khayr). Regarding who they are, there are two opinions:

First: they are the maidens (hur) created in the Hereafter.

Second: they are the virtuous believing women from the people of this world.

Regarding calling them khayrat (good ones), there are four aspects:

First: because they are good in character and beautiful in faces. This was said by Qatadah, and Umm Salamah related it as a marfuʿ (traced to the Prophet) report.

Second: because they are virgins, unspoiled. This was said by Abu Salih.

Third: because they are chosen.

Fourth: because they are good and righteous. This was said by Abu ʿUbaydah.

﴿Maidens restrained in pavilions.﴾ On this there are four interpretations:

First: restraining their gaze upon their husbands, so they do not desire any substitute for them and do not raise their glance to other men. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: those confined in private chambers (hijal), not wandering about in the roads. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: those secluded and protected, neither idle nor seeking display. This was said by Zayd ibn al-Harith and Abu ʿUbaydah.

Fourth: that they are those who dwell in palaces. This was said by al-Hasan.

A fifth possibility is that by al-maqsurat he means the white ones, derived from the polishing (qusarah) of white cloth, because the distinction between al-maqsurat and al-qasirat requires that there be a distinction between them in interpretation.

(p-443) Regarding al-khiyam (pavilions) there are three opinions:

First: that the pavilions are houses. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Second: that they are tents pitched for the people of Paradise outside Paradise, in the manner of the desert dwellings. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Third: that they are tents within Paradise that are attached to the palaces.

Ibn Masʿud related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The pavilions are hollow pearls." It is related from Asma' bint Yazid al-Ashhaliyyah that she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we women are confined and restrained, the foundations of your houses and the bearers of your children. Will we share in the reward?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes, if you are good to your husbands in their marital obligations and seek their pleasure."

﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾ (rafraf khudr). On this there are six interpretations:

First: that the rafraf is the enclosed seat surrounded by its carpets. This was said by Ibn Kamil.

Second: the surplus of cushions and rugs. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: that they are pillows. This was said by al-Hasan and ʿAsim al-Jahdari.

Fourth: that they are raised couches, derived from al-raff (shelf).

Fifth: that they are sitting places upon whose surplus they recline.

Sixth: the gardens of Paradise. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

﴿And ʿabqari (rich carpets) and beautiful ones.﴾ On this there are four opinions:

First: that they are velvet cushions. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: brocade. This was said by Mujahid.

(p-444) Third: that they are garments in Paradise that no one knows. This was also said by Mujahid.

Fourth: that they are the garments of this world, attributed to ʿAbqar.

Regarding ʿabqari (a word in the Arabic language meaning a superior of a people, or something surpassing its kind) there are two opinions:

First: that it means the chief of the people. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen anyone among the people as ʿabqari as he who excels (yafri farrahu)." So he attributed him to the finest garments because of his distinction.

Second: the land of ʿAbqar.

Regarding the naming of it by that, there are two opinions:

First: because of the abundance of jinn in it.

Second: because of the abundance of its sand. The meaning is that it is like the ʿabqari, because what is woven in ʿAbqar would not be in Paradise if it is said that ʿAbqar is the name of a land.

﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ (tabaraka ism rabbika). On this there are two aspects:

First: its meaning is that the name of your Lord is established and endures.

Second: that mentioning His name is a source of blessing and goodness, as encouragement to persist in remembering Him.

﴿Full of majesty and honour﴾ (dhi al-jalali wal-ikram). Regarding dhi al-jalal there are two aspects:

First: that He is the Majestic.

Second: that He is the one deserving of reverence and exaltation.

Regarding "al-ikram" there are two aspects:

First: the Generous.

Second: the one who bestows honour upon those who obey Him.

First: that the pavilions are houses. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Second: that they are tents pitched for the people of Paradise outside Paradise, in the manner of the desert dwellings. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Third: that they are tents within Paradise that are attached to the palaces.

Ibn Masʿud related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The pavilions are hollow pearls." It is related from Asma' bint Yazid al-Ashhaliyyah that she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we women are confined and restrained, the foundations of your houses and the bearers of your children. Will we share in the reward?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes, if you are good to your husbands in their marital obligations and seek their pleasure."

﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾ (rafraf khudr). On this there are six interpretations:

First: that the rafraf is the enclosed seat surrounded by its carpets. This was said by Ibn Kamil.

Second: the surplus of cushions and rugs. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: that they are pillows. This was said by al-Hasan and ʿAsim al-Jahdari.

Fourth: that they are raised couches, derived from al-raff (shelf).

Fifth: that they are sitting places upon whose surplus they recline.

Sixth: the gardens of Paradise. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

﴿And ʿabqari (rich carpets) and beautiful ones.﴾ On this there are four opinions:

First: that they are velvet cushions. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: brocade. This was said by Mujahid.

(p-444) Third: that they are garments in Paradise that no one knows. This was also said by Mujahid.

Fourth: that they are the garments of this world, attributed to ʿAbqar.

Regarding ʿabqari (a word in the Arabic language meaning a superior of a people, or something surpassing its kind) there are two opinions:

First: that it means the chief of the people. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen anyone among the people as ʿabqari as he who excels (yafri farrahu)." So he attributed him to the finest garments because of his distinction.

Second: the land of ʿAbqar.

Regarding the naming of it by that, there are two opinions:

First: because of the abundance of jinn in it.

Second: because of the abundance of its sand. The meaning is that it is like the ʿabqari, because what is woven in ʿAbqar would not be in Paradise if it is said that ʿAbqar is the name of a land.

﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ (tabaraka ism rabbika). On this there are two aspects:

First: its meaning is that the name of your Lord is established and endures.

Second: that mentioning His name is a source of blessing and goodness, as encouragement to persist in remembering Him.

﴿Full of majesty and honour﴾ (dhi al-jalali wal-ikram). Regarding dhi al-jalal there are two aspects:

First: that He is the Majestic.

Second: that He is the one deserving of reverence and exaltation.

Regarding "al-ikram" there are two aspects:

First: the Generous.

Second: the one who bestows honour upon those who obey Him.
